claim: RNA-catalyzed RNA replication is widely considered a key step in the emergence of life's first genetic system.
source: RNA-catalyzed RNA replication is widely considered a key step in the emergence of life's first genetic system.
evidence: This is a statement about scientific consensus in the field, representing established knowledge in origin of life research.

claim: RNA replication can be impeded by the extraordinary stability of duplex RNA products.
source: RNA replication can be impeded by the extraordinary stability of duplex RNA products, which must be dissociated for re-initiation of the next replication cycle.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the strand separation problem in RNA replication.

claim: A triplet polymerase ribozyme can catalyze sustained rolling circle synthesis beyond full-length circle synthesis with strand displacement.
source: We observe sustained RCS by a triplet polymerase ribozyme beyond full-length circle synthesis with strand displacement yielding concatemeric RNA products.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in the manuscript figures.

claim: Rolling circle synthesis by a triplet polymerase ribozyme yields concatemeric RNA products.
source: We observe sustained RCS by a triplet polymerase ribozyme beyond full-length circle synthesis with strand displacement yielding concatemeric RNA products.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: A circular Hammerhead ribozyme is capable of self-cleavage.
source: Furthermore, we show RCS of a circular Hammerhead ribozyme capable of self-cleavage and re-circularization.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: A circular Hammerhead ribozyme is capable of re-circularization.
source: Furthermore, we show RCS of a circular Hammerhead ribozyme capable of self-cleavage and re-circularization.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: All steps of a viroid-like RNA replication pathway can be catalyzed by RNA alone.
source: Thus, all steps of a viroid-like RNA replication pathway can be catalyzed by RNA alone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Rolling circle synthesis leads to progressive build-up of conformational strain.
source: Finally, we explore potential RCS mechanisms by molecular dynamics simulations, which indicate a progressive build-up of conformational strain upon RCS with destabilization of nascent strand 5′- and 3′-ends.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Rolling circle synthesis causes destabilization of nascent strand 5′-ends.
source: Finally, we explore potential RCS mechanisms by molecular dynamics simulations, which indicate a progressive build-up of conformational strain upon RCS with destabilization of nascent strand 5′- and 3′-ends.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Rolling circle synthesis causes destabilization of nascent strand 3′-ends.
source: Finally, we explore potential RCS mechanisms by molecular dynamics simulations, which indicate a progressive build-up of conformational strain upon RCS with destabilization of nascent strand 5′- and 3′-ends.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: RNA catalysis plays an essential role in present-day biology.
source: Such hypotheses of an 'RNA world'—a primordial biology centered on RNA as the main biomolecule—are in accord with the essential role of RNA catalysis in present-day biology (Cech, 2000; Goldman and Kacar, 2021; Nissen et al., 2000; Wilkinson et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Multiple prebiotic synthetic pathways to RNA nucleotides have been discovered.
source: and the discovery of multiple prebiotic synthetic pathways to several of the RNA (and DNA) nucleotides (Becker et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2020; Patel et al., 2015; Powner et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: RNA polymerase ribozymes can perform templated RNA synthesis of up to ~200 nucleotides.
source: RNA in vitro evolution and engineering have led to the discovery of RNA polymerase ribozymes (RPRs) able to perform templated RNA synthesis of up to ~200 nucleotides (nt) (Attwater et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RNA polymerase ribozymes can synthesize active ribozymes including the catalytic class I ligase core.
source: synthesizing active ribozymes including the catalytic class I ligase core (Horning and Joyce, 2016; Tjhung et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A triplet polymerase ribozyme displays enhanced capacity to copy highly structured RNA templates.
source: An RPR capable of utilizing trinucleotide triphosphates (triplets) as substrates (a triplet polymerase ribozyme [TPR]) has been shown to display an enhanced capacity to copy highly structured RNA templates including segments of its own sequence (Attwater et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The strand separation problem is a central obstacle to autonomous RNA self-replication.
source: Nevertheless, there remain a number of fundamental obstacles to be overcome before an autonomous self-replication system can be established. A central problem among these is the so-called 'strand separation problem,' a form of product inhibition due to the accumulation of highly stable dead-end RNA duplexes, which cannot be dissociated (efficiently) under replication conditions (Le Vay and Mutschler, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The strand separation problem has been overcome by PCR-like thermocycling.
source: The strand separation problem has been overcome by PCR-like thermocycling (or thermophoresis) (Horning and Joyce, 2016; Salditt et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Thermocycling approaches to strand separation may be limited to short RNA oligomers.
source: but this approach may be limited to short RNA oligomers (even in the presence of high concentrations of denaturing agents) as the melting temperatures of longer RNA duplexes approach or even exceed the boiling point of water (Freier et al., 1986; Szostak, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents a logical inference from the properties of RNA duplexes.

claim: The melting temperatures of longer RNA duplexes approach or exceed the boiling point of water.
source: as the melting temperatures of longer RNA duplexes approach or even exceed the boiling point of water (Freier et al., 1986; Szostak, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Circular genomes are widespread in biology including eukaryotes, prokaryotes, and viruses.
source: Circular rather than linear genomes are widespread in biology including eukaryotes, prokaryotes, and viruses (Moller et al., 2018; Moss et al., 2020; Shulman and Davidson, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Circular RNAs are found as products of RNA splicing.
source: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are found as products of RNA splicing (Kristensen et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RNA-based self-circularization is known in multiple ribozymes.
source: and RNA-based self-circularization is known in multiple ribozymes (Hieronymus and Müller, 2019; Lasda and Parker, 2014; Petkovic and Müller, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Rolling circle synthesis is found in the replication of RNA genomes in some viruses and viroids.
source: Continuous templated RNA synthesis on circular templates (rolling circle synthesis [RCS]) is also widespread and found in the replication of the RNA genomes in some viruses and in viroids.
evidence: This represents established knowledge in virology.

claim: Viroid RNA replication has been proposed to resemble an ancient mechanism for replication.
source: Indeed, viroid RNA replication has been proposed to resemble an ancient mechanism for replication (Diener, 1989; Flores et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In idealized rolling circle synthesis, strand invasion and displacement processes are isoenergetic.
source: In an idealized RCS mechanism, both strand invasion and displacement processes are isoenergetic and coordinated to nascent strand extension (Blanco et al., 1989; Daubendiek et al., 1995)
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents theoretical understanding of the mechanism.

claim: Rotation of single-stranded RNA alleviates the build-up of topological tension during rolling circle synthesis.
source: with rotation of the single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) alleviating the build-up of topological tension (Kuhn et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Rolling circle synthesis is a potentially open-ended process leading to synthesis of single-stranded multiple repeat products.
source: Thus, RCS is a potentially open-ended process leading to the synthesis of single-stranded multiple repeat products (concatemers) with an internally energized strand displacement (Tupper and Higgs, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents theoretical understanding.

claim: Triplet binding to the template strand and dissociation of an equal trinucleotide stretch from the 5′-end are both equilibrium processes and nearly isoenergetic.
source: Triplet binding to the template strand and dissociation of an equal trinucleotide stretch from the 5′-end are both equilibrium processes and nearly isoenergetic.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference about the energetics of the process.

claim: Extension (ligation of bound triplet to growing 3′-end) is an irreversible step in rolling circle synthesis.
source: However, extension (i.e., ligation of the bound triplet to the growing 3′-end) is an irreversible step.
evidence: This is based on understanding of the chemical mechanism.

claim: Rolling circle synthesis proceeds in ratchet-like fashion with strand displacement driven by triphosphate hydrolysis and triplet ligation.
source: Thus, in this scenario, RCS would be expected to proceed in ratchet-like fashion with strand displacement driven by triphosphate hydrolysis and triplet ligation.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference about the mechanism.

claim: Circularized RNA is resistant to exonuclease T digestion.
source: Only circRNA is resistant to ExoT digestion.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel data in Figure 1B.

claim: The TPR comprises a catalytic subunit (5TU) and a non-catalytic subunit (t1).
source: Schematic representation of primer triplet extension on a linear or circRNA template and of the TPR hetero-dimer comprising the catalytic subunit (5TU (green)) and the non-catalytic subunit (t1 (red)) (Attwater et al., 2018)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C, with citation to prior work.

claim: The TPR can perform primer extension on circular RNA templates.
source: PAGE gel of TPR primer extension, P9 (5′-FAM-GAAGAAGAA) is the unextended primer, bands 1–9 denote extension of P9 by +1 to + 9 triplets (full length).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel data in Figure 1D.

claim: Extension efficiency on circular RNA templates shows a periodic banding pattern matching the helical pitch of double-stranded RNA.
source: Furthermore, we observed a periodic banding pattern of triplet extension efficiency matching the helical pitch of double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) (11.3 base pairs (bp)/turn Bhattacharyya et al., 1990; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 1E and supported by citation.

claim: Double-stranded RNA has a helical pitch of 11.3 base pairs per turn.
source: matching the helical pitch of double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) (11.3 base pairs (bp)/turn Bhattacharyya et al., 1990; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Triplet junctions located on the inside of the scRNA ring are less easily accessible than in linear RNA.
source: Presumably, triplet junctions located on the inside of the scRNA ring are less easily accessible and therefore less efficiently ligated than in linear RNA, which is freely accessible from all sides (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural model shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Full circle extension products were obtained for multiple templates ranging from 34 to 58 nt in size.
source: Despite the reduced extension efficiency in scRNA, we obtained full circle extension products for multiple templates (34–58 nt in size, Figure 2A and B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel data in Figure 2B.

claim: Mean extension efficiency for circular templates increases with increasing template size.
source: with a clear trend toward increasing mean extension efficiency for circular templates with increasing size predicting parity with the linear template at around 120 nt (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data plotted in Figure 2C.

claim: Extension efficiency for circular templates is predicted to reach parity with linear templates at around 120 nt.
source: with a clear trend toward increasing mean extension efficiency for circular templates with increasing size predicting parity with the linear template at around 120 nt (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the trend shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Primer extension can proceed beyond full circle requiring duplex invasion and displacement of the primer/product strand.
source: We observed an extension of up to +3 triplets (+9) above the full circle mark (Figure 2B, lanes 7–12), indicating displacement of the primer 5′-end upon incorporation of three additional pppGAA triplets.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel data in Figure 2B.

claim: Synthesis beyond full circle including strand displacement is possible on scRNA templates.
source: This indicated that synthesis beyond full circle including strand displacement is possible on scRNA templates, boding well for the implementation of RCS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Greater dilution of reaction mixtures prior to freezing results in more efficient strand displacement.
source: Interestingly, greater dilution of reaction mixtures prior to freezing resulted in more efficient stand displacement.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the data.

claim: Greater pre-freezing dilution increases the eutectic phase/ice interface area.
source: While greater pre-freezing dilution does not alter the final solute concentrations within the eutectic phase (Attwater et al., 2010), it increases the eutectic phase/ice interface area.
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents understanding of eutectic phase behavior.

claim: Strand invasion may be aided by surface effects at the eutectic phase/ice interface.
source: This suggests that strand invasion may be aided by surface effects, as previously suggested for RNA refolding (Mutschler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Progressive accumulation of progressively longer RCS products was observed over prolonged reaction times up to 6 weeks.
source: Under these optimized buffer and extension conditions, we observed progressive accumulation of progressively longer RCS products, over prolonged reaction times (up to 6 weeks) (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel data in Figure 2D.

claim: Reaction speed decreases after approximately 4 weeks incubation.
source: with reaction speed decreasing after ca. 4 weeks incubation, indicating continued RCS over extended periods of time (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the kinetic data in Figure 2E and F.

claim: As dsRNA is elongated during rolling circle synthesis, the remaining ssRNA segment of the scRNA becomes increasingly extended.
source: The simulation trajectories revealed the high energy barrier of dsRNA for bending and accommodating a circular shape (Figure 3A). Instead, we observe that, as dsRNA is elongated, the remaining ssRNA segment of the scRNA becomes increasingly extended.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the molecular dynamics simulation data in Figure 3A.

claim: When the dsRNA part reaches 27 bp, torsional strain is relieved by dissociation of the dsRNA 5′- and 3′-ends.
source: As the dsRNA part reaches 27 bp (corresponding to band 6 in Figure 1D), the ssRNA segment was fully extended and torsional strain was relieved by dissociation (peeling off) of the dsRNA 5′- and 3′-ends rather than by bending or the introduction of kinks into the dsRNA segment (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the molecular dynamics simulation data in Figure 3B.

claim: Multiple peeling off and rebinding events were observed during the MD trajectories indicating fast dynamics.
source: Subsequently, multiple peeling off and rebinding events were observed during the trajectories indicating that the dynamics of this process are fast (Videos 1 and 2 and Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the molecular dynamics simulation data in Videos 1 and 2.

claim: An inhibitory effect was observed for insertion of the final triplets into the scRNA template.
source: In the experimental data, we also observed an inhibitory effect for insertion of the final triplets (+8, +9, and +10 (beyond full length)/extension to 33, 36, and 39 nt of RNA in Figure 2D) into the corresponding scRNA template.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data in Figure 2D.

claim: The onset of 3′- and 5′-ends destabilization may attenuate primer extension by the ribozyme.
source: This may indeed reflect the onset of the 3′- and 5′-ends destabilization observed in the MD simulations (Figure 3), which would likely attenuate primer extension by the ribozyme.
evidence: This is an inference connecting simulation and experimental data.

claim: Extension efficiency recovered beyond full length although at lower speed.
source: Note however that the extension efficiency recovered beyond full length (+11/extension to 41 nt, Figure 2F), although at lower speed (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: A linear RNA molecule with a nick does not show base opening or dissociation at 5′- or 3′-strand ends.
source: As a control for the observed dsRNA end destabilization mechanism, we also ran an MD simulation of a linear RNA molecule containing four consecutive triplets with a nick between two of them, but observed neither base opening nor dissociation at either 5′- or 3′-strand ends (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the molecular dynamics simulation control data.

claim: Groove dimensions and local helical parameters for RCS simulations on circular RNA did not show major adjustment compared with linear RNA control.
source: Groove dimensions and local helical parameters (roll, twist, and slide) for the RCS simulations on circular RNA did not show any major adjustment compared with the linear RNA control (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Simulations at different Mg2+ and K+ concentrations did not show major differences in dsRNA strand dissociation or bending.
source: To mirror the experimental eutectic phase conditions, simulations were run at relatively high Mg2+ concentrations (100 mM) and compared with the presence of monovalent ions like K+ (200 mM) and high concentration of Mg2+ (500 mM), but simulations did not show any major differences in terms of dsRNA strand dissociation or bending (Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Mg2+ ions interact more strongly with different parts of RNA compared to K+ ions.
source: However, Mg2+ ions—compared to K+—appear to interact more strongly with different parts of the RNA and, consequently, may increase the probability of distorted conformations facilitating the exposition of nucleobases at the 5′- and 3′-ends.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the molecular dynamics simulation data in Figure 3C.

claim: K+ ions are mainly positioned as counterions along the major and minor groove.
source: In contrast, K+ ions are mainly positioned as counterions along the major and minor groove, allowing the bases to orient toward the inside of the dsRNA helix for base-pairing interactions (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Increasing MgCl2 concentration to 500 mM does not bring extra stabilization as the system appears saturated at 100 mM Mg2+.
source: However, increasing MgCl2 concentration to 500 mM does not seem to bring extra stabilization, as the system appears to be saturated already at 100 mM Mg2+ (Figure 3—figure supplements 5 and 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Progressive RNA synthesis on a scRNA template leads to increased dynamics of nucleobase exposure.
source: In summary, our simulations support the notion that progressive RNA synthesis on a scRNA template (in the presence of Mg2+ ions) leads to increased dynamics of nucleobase exposure, RNA duplex destabilization, and 5′- and 3′-ends melting.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: A small circular fully dsRNA molecule is implausible due to the prohibitive energetic cost of dsRNA bending.
source: The simulations also clearly illustrate the implausibility of a small circular fully dsRNA molecule (as schematically illustrated in Figure 1E), due to the prohibitive energetic cost of dsRNA bending.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The system relieves internal strain by extending the ssRNA segment of the circle and peeling of both dsRNA 5′- and 3′-ends.
source: Instead, the system appears to relieve internal strain by extending the ssRNA segment of the circle (partially shielding the dsRNA segment) and peeling of both dsRNA 5′- and 3′-ends (Figure 3)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the molecular dynamics simulation data in Figure 3.

claim: Dynamic destabilization of dsRNA 5′-ends has the potential to facilitate strand displacement during RNA replication on a scRNA template.
source: Dynamic destabilization of dsRNA 5′-ends clearly has the potential to facilitate strand displacement during RNA replication on a scRNA template (and may aid continuous RCS)
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation data.

claim: Dynamic destabilization of dsRNA ends may reduce the efficiency of primer extension by reducing availability of the primer 3′-end.
source: but at the same time may reduce the efficiency of primer extension and triplet incorporation by reducing the availability of the primer 3′-end and the downstream template bases.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation data.

claim: These effects would be predicted to manifest in RNA circles up to 200 bp as suggested by RNA persistence length.
source: These effects would be predicted to manifest themselves in RNA circles up to 200 bp as suggested by RNA persistence length (Abels et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to prior work on RNA persistence length.

claim: All four barcoded templates yielded longer than full-length products indicative of continued RNA synthesis beyond full length.
source: Further, all templates yielded longer than full-length products indicative of continued RNA synthesis by the TPR beyond full length (positions>9).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sequencing data in Figure 4B.

claim: Fidelity dropped after full length was reached, indicative of significant non-templated terminal transferase-like activity.
source: However, the fidelity dropped after full length was reached, indicative of significant non-templated terminal transferase-like (TT) activity in this regime (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sequencing data in Figure 4B.

claim: The average fidelity for insertion of the expected triplet at position 10 for circular templates was 10.9%.
source: For example, the average fidelity for insertion of the expected triplet (pppGAA) for position 10 (full length +1) for circular templates was 10.9%
evidence: This is calculated from the sequencing data.

claim: The fidelity at position 9 (full length) for circular templates was 89.9%.
source: whereas for position 9 (full length) it was 89.9%.
evidence: This is calculated from the sequencing data.

claim: For linear templates, the fidelity for full length +1 dropped to 0.7%.
source: For linear templates, the fidelity for full length +1 dropped to 0.7%
evidence: This is calculated from the sequencing data.

claim: The fidelity at full length for linear templates was 78.8%.
source: compared to full length 78.8%.
evidence: This is calculated from the sequencing data.

claim: The probability of a product extending to longer than full length with correct sequence was 10-100-fold higher for circular compared to linear RNA templates.
source: For this reason, the probability of a product extending to longer than full length (positions 10–12) with the correct sequence was 10–100-fold higher for circular compared to linear RNA templates (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is calculated from the sequencing data and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Extension beyond full length on circular templates continued to insert barcode triplets correctly up to position 18.
source: On all circular templates (with the exception of template B, where too few reads were obtained) extension beyond full length (while containing a significant TT component) continued to insert the barcode triplets correctly, indicating continuous RCS at least up to position 18 (63 nt, more than 1.5 times full-length circle synthesis on the scRNA template).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sequencing data in Figure 4B.

claim: Dilution appears to aid strand invasion fidelity and continued templated synthesis.
source: Interestingly, non-diluted samples had a decreased fidelity at position 10 (the point of strand invasion) compared to diluted samples (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) suggesting that dilution appears to aid not only extension efficiency (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), but also strand invasion fidelity and continued templated synthesis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: These results are consistent with RNA-catalyzed RCS on scRNA templates beyond the full circle.
source: In summary, these results are consistent with RNA-catalyzed RCS on scRNA templates beyond the full circle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the sequencing data.

claim: A higher degree of RCS with strand displacement was observed with double priming on the circular RNA template.
source: Indeed, we observed a higher degree of RCS with strand displacement with the 36 nt scRNA template termed sc8211 having two identical primer sites leading to two different products being formed (product I or II) (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel data in Figure 5B.

claim: When all triplets were present, extension continued to beyond full circle.
source: Finally, when all triplets (pppGAA, pppAUA, pppCGC, and pppCUG) were present, extension continued to beyond full circle (positions≥10) (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel data in Figure 5B.

claim: Bands corresponding to extension products exceeding two times full-length circle synthesis were observed.
source: and bands corresponding to extension products exceeding two times full-length circle synthesis (>triplet 21 (63 nt)) of replication were observed (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel data in Figure 5C.

claim: Sequencing identified long reads including many with 15 correct triplet incorporations representing ~1.5 times full-length circle synthesis.
source: Sequencing of the long, branched RCS RNA products (excised from gel band corresponding to ≥15 triplets, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) identified a range of long reads (from both products I and II) including many reads of the product with 15 correct triplet incorporations (Figure 5E) representing ~1.5 times full-length circle synthesis (n: 7×103 and 1×105 reads of products I and II, respectively).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sequencing data in Figure 5D.

claim: The longest products comprised 29 correct triplet incorporations (96 nt) representing RCS of >2.5 times full-length circle synthesis.
source: However, much longer sequences were present in decreasing numbers of reads, with the longest products comprising 29 correct triplet incorporations (96 nt) (n=2) representing RCS of >2.5 times full-length circle synthesis and the longest reported product synthesised by the TPR.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sequencing data in Figure 5D.

claim: 96 nt products represent the longest reported product synthesized by the TPR.
source: with the longest products comprising 29 correct triplet incorporations (96 nt) (n=2) representing RCS of >2.5 times full-length circle synthesis and the longest reported product synthesised by the TPR.
evidence: This is stated as a factual claim about the record for this ribozyme.

claim: Freeze-thaw cycles enhance ribozyme activity by affecting RNA refolding.
source: Freeze-thaw (FT) cycles have been previously shown to enhance ribozyme activity by affecting RNA refolding (Mutschler et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Inclusion of four freeze-thaw cycles led to more efficient production of longer RCS RNA products.
source: and indeed inclusion of four FT cycles lead to more efficient production of longer RCS RNA products (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel data in Figures 5B and C.

claim: Isothermal branched RCS yields long concatemeric products comprising >2.5 tandem repeats of the scRNA template.
source: In summary, isothermal branched RCS yields long concatemeric products comprising >2.5 tandem repeats of the scRNA template with RCS efficiency further enhanced by FT cycling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Viroids are transcriptional parasites composed entirely of a circular RNA genome.
source: Viroids are transcriptional parasites composed entirely of a circular RNA genome and are considered the simplest infectious pathogens known in nature.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about viroids.

claim: Viroids are considered the simplest infectious pathogens known in nature.
source: Viroids are transcriptional parasites composed entirely of a circular RNA genome and are considered the simplest infectious pathogens known in nature.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about viroids.

claim: Viroids lack protein-coding regions in their genome.
source: They lack protein-coding regions in their genome and can be completely replicated in ribosome-free conditions (Daròs et al., 1994; Diener, 2003; Fadda et al., 2003; Flores et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Viroids can be completely replicated in ribosome-free conditions.
source: They lack protein-coding regions in their genome and can be completely replicated in ribosome-free conditions (Daròs et al., 1994; Diener, 2003; Fadda et al., 2003; Flores et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Avsunviroidae can comprise a circular RNA genome of as little as ~300 nt encoding a Hammerhead ribozyme.
source: They can comprise a circular RNA genome of as little as ~300 nt in, for example, Avsunviroidae encoding a Hammerhead ribozyme responsible for maturation by resecting the replicated RNA genome (Flores et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The resected viroid genome is ligated (circularized) by a host protein such as tRNA ligase.
source: The resected viroid genome is then ligated (circularized) by a host protein (e.g., tRNA ligase) (Nohales et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Circular RNA genomes present increased stability by end protection.
source: Indeed, circular RNA genomes would present a number of potential advantages for prebiotic RNA replication, including increased stability by end protection (Litke and Jaffrey, 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Circular RNA genomes have a reduced requirement for specific primer oligonucleotides to sustain replication.
source: and a reduced requirement for specific primer oligonucleotides to sustain replication (Attwater et al., 2018; Szostak, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A circular RNA genome resolves the end replication problem.
source: A circular RNA genome also resolves the end replication problem, that is, the potential loss of genetic information from incomplete replication in linear genomes.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the properties of circular genomes.

claim: Circular RNA structures can self-assemble from RNA mononucleotides through wet-dry cycling.
source: Circular RNA structures can self-assemble from RNA mononucleotides through wet-dry cycling (Hassenkam et al., 2020) providing potential initiation points for primordial RNA replication.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: RNA can perform RCS on scRNA templates yielding concatemeric RNA products.
source: Our data show that RNA can indeed perform RCS on scRNA templates yielding concatemeric RNA products, which can be processed (i.e., resected) and re-circularized by an encoded ribozyme in a scheme reminiscent of viroid replication.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Concatemeric RNA products can be processed and re-circularized by an encoded ribozyme.
source: Our data show that RNA can indeed perform RCS on scRNA templates yielding concatemeric RNA products, which can be processed (i.e., resected) and re-circularized by an encoded ribozyme in a scheme reminiscent of viroid replication.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: One-half of a viroid replication cycle can be carried out by just two ribozymes.
source: Thus, one-half of a viroid replication cycle ((−)-strand replication leading to a self-circularizing (+)-strand) can be carried out by just two ribozymes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Completing a full viroid replication cycle would require the reverse (+)-strand replication leading to a self-circularizing (−)-strand product.
source: Completing a full viroid replication cycle would then require the reverse (+)-strand replication leading to a self-circularizing (−)-strand product.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be needed for a complete cycle.

claim: Topological strain-induced strand displacement may be general and independent of the precise RCS mechanism on scRNA templates.
source: This topological strain-induced strand displacement may be general and independent of the precise RCS mechanism on scRNA templates and thus should also apply to non-enzymatic polymerization of RNA.
evidence: This is a speculative inference from the simulation data.

claim: Branched extension, freeze-thaw thermocycling, and pre-freezing dilution may enhance RCS through accelerating conformational equilibration.
source: Our observation that RCS can be enhanced by the use of branched extension, FT thermocycling, and pre-freezing dilution may also be related to this. Indeed, while the precise mechanistic basis for these enhancements is currently unknown, it seems plausible that all of these enhance 5′-end displacement on the product strand by accelerating conformational equilibration through RNA un- and refolding as observed previously (Mutschler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Viroid and Hepatitis D virus replication proceeds through RCS on circular RNA genomes mediated by proteinaceous RNA polymerases.
